title: The Metamorphosis
description: Kafka's 1915 novella about a salesman who wakes as a giant insect, and a family that learns it can live without him.

chunks.text: Gregor is loved as long as he earns. Once he cannot, his family discovers it can live without him.
The change is never explained. Kafka cares only about what everyone does next.
The family is happiest on the morning after his death.
The opening reports the impossible as plain fact. Gregor's first worries are not his body but his job and the train he will miss: the self that work made survives the body.
chunks.source_quote: One morning, when Gregor Samsa woke from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a horrible vermin.

chunks.text: There is no waking from it. Kafka closes the door on allegory in the first page: this is happening, and the story is about living with it.
chunks.source_quote: "What's happened to me?" he thought. It wasn't a dream.

chunks.text: Even transformed, Gregor complains about his profession first. Work is the frame through which he sees everything, including his own catastrophe.
chunks.source_quote: "Oh, God", he thought, "what a strenuous career it is that I've chosen!"

chunks.text: The last image belongs to Grete, not Gregor. The family rides out of the city, plans a smaller flat and a husband for her; his death has given them back their lives.
chunks.source_quote: Grete was the first to get up and stretch out her young body.

chunks.text: Peace Treaty Architecture argues that partnership must rest on mutual need. The Samsas show the weak form of that need: dependence on one member's wages, which ends the moment he can no longer earn.
In Peculiarities of Planetary Conquest, people are judged inhuman by their gestures and killed for it. Gregor's family reaches the same verdict about him, more slowly and with more guilt.

The Metamorphosis is usually read as a story about alienation, but its sharpest observations are about the family as an economy. Gregor has paid his father's debts for years; the transformation simply ends the payments. What follows is a slow recalculation: the father goes back to work, the mother and sister take jobs, and the room that housed the breadwinner becomes a storeroom for a burden.

Kafka never decides whether Gregor is still human inside, and the family never asks. That silence is the point. Once a person's value is measured by what they provide, the question of who they are stops being asked, and the story's quiet ending, a pleasant tram ride in the sun, is its cruelest page.
